confidence_why: Whitman 1947 describes a free, contrastive accent on one of the first two syllables with minimal pairs, Greer 2016 and Hamilton and Irvin 1848 independently confirm that accent distinguishes words, and the only dissent, the weight-sensitive second-mora coding in StressTyp2 and WALS taken from Hayes 1995 and Miner 1979 (as summarized by Helmbrecht 2010), is a comparative-historical analysis whose own author states that vowel length has been lost and accent is now phonemic.

catalog_quote: 7. Primary and secondary accent. The Ioway language has a free primary accent on one of the first two syllables of a word. It is of the type of a rather light stress accompanied by slight lengthening of the accented vowel. It is capable of distinguishing otherwise identical words, e.g., añį́ he has, áñį I have; wañį́ meat, wáñį he has them; añásgų he had it, it seems, áñàsgų they said it, it seems. ... There is regularly a shift of accent from the first to the second syllable of a two syllable stem in word composition when there is amalgamation (see below) at the point of junction ... Ioway has two types of secondary accent. The first is rhythmically determined by the position of the primary accent and falls on the third syllable after the one bearing the primary accent. Since this accent is not capable of characterizing words and is automatically determined, it is ignored in our transc…
sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for iowa1245: Miner 1979, 'Dorsey's Law in Winnebago-Chiwere and Winnebago Accent', IJAL 45(1):25-33 (already listed; still-to-obtain as paywalled in the 16 Sep check). It is relevant (contains Chiwere accented cognate data and the comparative claim that Chiwere keeps second-syllable/mora accent, and is a WALS/StressTyp data source for 'Oto'), but its main subject is Winnebago accent. No open copy exists: publisher landing and PDF could not be reached by automated download, JSTOR is bot-blocked, archive. Access = paywalled (online with a university library loginvia the Harvard library catalogue); priority medium. What it says was recovered second-hand from the held Helmbrecht 2010 chapter (pp. 119, 123-124, Tables 5-6 citing Miner 1979:27, 31): Chiwere accent on the second syllable/mora, unshifted, versus Hocak's third-mora accent; Greer 2016 fn. 7 cites Miner only for Dorsey's Law and Hall & Niederecker 2019 only for Winnebago epenthetic-vowel accent. None of this changes the catalog: the 'lexical' coding rests on Whitman 1947 sec. 7 (free, contrastive accent on one of the first two syllables; length non-phonemic), corroborated by Greer 2016 sec. 2.3, and the Miner-Hayes-StressTyp second-mora/weight analysis is already recorded as a diachronic 'contra' line. Files (search-result pages) and logged in there. Acquiring Miner 1979 (one the Harvard library catalogue download) would let the record quote his Chiwere accent data directly and state precisely why the peninitial-plus-weight analysis is comparative rather than synchronic.

new_statements.quote: The second important correspondence Dorsey found was the regular stress shift from the second syllable or mora in Chiwere to the third syllable or mora in Hocak. ... [Table 6, cf. Miner 1979: 31: Chiwere] wasóse 'brave', agúje 'footwear', mišcį́Ne 'Hare', wanáxe 'spirit', inúwenaha 'second'. ... Hocak has undergone a stress shift one mora to the right at one point in its history, while its closest relative, Chiwere, did not. All other Siouan languages have main stress on the second syllable or second mora (there is some variation, but none has the rules found in Hocak).

new_statements.reading: This is NOT a first-hand description of Chiwere: it is a Hocak specialist's second-hand summary of the comparative-Siouan position (Dorsey 1883, Miner 1979) that Chiwere accent sits on the second syllable/mora of the word, illustrated with five Chiwere forms from Miner 1979:31 that are all accented on the second syllable. It is the only new stress-relevant text actually read in this search of works with stress in the title (nothing by Miner 1979 itself could be opened). It supports the catalog's existing 'contra' note that the weight/mora analysis (Hayes 1995:356, StressTyp1 'initial if heavy else peninitial') is a comparative-diachronic reading, and it is compatible with Whitman's data (Whitman's initial-accent words are 1sg-coalescence cases, i.e. long first vowels under a moraic count) but says nothing about the synchronic phonemic contrasts (añį́ vs áñį; ráwe vs rawé) on which the 'lexical' coding rests. It does not displace Whitman 1947 sec. 7 as the deciding source.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Reader's bearing stands with three refinements. (1) Helmbrecht 2010 is a Hocak description (his own data are Hocak field notes, the DoBeS corpus, Susman 1943, Miner 1979/1990; p. 120 sec. 2); every Chiwere form and every statement about Chiwere accent is attributed to Dorsey 1883 or Miner 1979: 27, 31 — it contains no first-hand Chiwere evidence. readall_conflicts: No new first-hand text was opened, so nothing read contradicts the catalog. Two secondary readings sit beside it: (a) WALS (citing Miner 1979 + Whitman 1947) codes Oto as 'No fixed stress' / 'Left-edge: First or second' / weight factor 'Long vowel', i.e. weight-sensitive rather than fixed peninitial; this is compatible with the catalog's peninitial rule if the initial-stress cases are long-first-vowel (contracted 1sg / wa-+locative) forms, as the existing Helmbrecht-based note already argues; (b) the on-disk Greer/GoodTracks draft sketch (2010-2012, sec. 1.1d) asserts that stress is phonemic in Baxoje-Jiwere but leaves its minimal-pair example blank ('XXXX') and says the accent 'may shift to the right' in words of 3+ syllables when affixes are added, and that wa-+locative fusions make a 'heavy' long-vowel syllable that 'usually attracts stress' (lines 248-268, 750-751 of). Neither displaces Whitman 1947 sec. 7 / StressTyp2 as the deciding source; the WALS coding and Greer both point toward a weight/lexical component that the catalog already flags in its contra note.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Whitman 1947:238 sec. 7) is present verbatim on the page scan we hold; the Greer 2016 pp. 187-188 secondary statements are present verbatim in the extracted text we hold. (2) Deciding source: a 1947 IJAL descriptive grammar (sketch-length) from fluent-speaker fieldwork, corroborated by the 2016 LangSci sketch, by Greer's 2010-12 draft sketch (downloaded now) and by the 1848 missionary grammar (downloaded now: 1sg vs 3sg distinguished by accent on 1st vs 2nd/3rd syllable). No modern phonology article, dissertation or instrumental study of Chiwere stress exists; the language has had no fluent speakers since 1996. (3) The only rival analysis is the comparative-Siouan/metrical one (Miner 1979 -> Hayes 1995 -> StressTyp1 'initial if heavy else peninitial'), and StressTyp's own source passage and note say vowel length is lost and synchronic accent is phonemic/lexical

sources.quote: 'That illustration is evidence that stress is a meaningful (phonemic) quality in Baxoje-Jiwere. ... When a root word with two syllables has additional prefixes or suffixes attached to it, the basic stress pattern can change. In these cases, the accent may shift to the "right" or later in the word, especially if there are 3 or more syllables.' On length: 'no phonemic distinction in Jiwere-Baxoje vowel length has been documented' (Rankin heard length on recordings; Greer could not).

tone.quote: Stress or accent in a language refers to patterned and regular use of sound differences as another method of telling similar-sounding words apart from one another. The relative “loudness” or increased volume of one syllable versus another can distinguish between words that otherwise sound exactly the same. In addition to the volume, there can also be a change in the pitch or “height” of the tone which helps the listener notice that syllable more easily, and unstressed syllables tend to have lower pitch than stressed ones. [...] That illustration is evidence that stress is a meaningful (phonemic) quality in Baxoje-Jiwere.
